3832.prule: Culminative stress whose locus is set by morpheme identity, with a two-way lexical tone contrast (high/falling vs rising) realized on the stressed syllable. Roots are canonically a single CVC syllable carrying the one stress/tone locus; the rare bisyllabic (CV1CV1C) and reduplicated roots take the single locus on the second syllable 'almost without exception'. In inflected verbs the domain (verb-complex positions 2/3-26) carries one or two primary stress/tone loci, normally on the obligatory boundary suffix and/or the syllable preceding it, the choice being lexically determined by that suffix; root+-VC suffix combinations take one or two loci 'lexically conditioned by the suffix'. In nominals the domain is the noun phrase (positions 5-15) and 'the identity of elements as roots, adjectives, classifiers, or particular suffixes determines which syllables will attract stress'; stress is normally culminative but some suffixes are lexically marked for an additional stress. Right-oriented (boundary suffix) but not counted from a word edge and not weight-sensitive.
3832.srule: Not mentioned in Epps 2024 (§2 p. 450, §5.1 pp. 470-471, §5.5 pp. 473-474 read: only one or two PRIMARY stress/tone loci per domain). 3832.tone: Two contrastive tones, 'realized on stressed syllables' (p. 450): acute = high tone or its falling allophone, hacek = rising tone (fn. 2). conflict.would_settle: No observation can settle it (script-only language, extinct c. 1st c. AD; neither Iberian script nor Latin marks accent, and Ballester himself notes Latin adaptations cannot show oxytones). What could move the record is a third specialist treatment that weighs both reconstructions: the unread phonology monograph Quintanilla 1998, Estudios de fonología ibérica (bibliography row 7, print only, no link) — if it treats accent at all — or the unread current synthesis Moncunill & Velaza 2019 'Iberian' in Sinner & Velaza eds., OUP (bibliography row 5, paywalled DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198790822.001.0001), which would show whether the field has adopted either position or regards accent as unrecoverable (in which case the record would become undeterminable rather than resolved). The only primary evidence class that discriminates final from penultimate is the handful of Greek accentuations of Iberian names (e.g. Σαιταβί in Ptolemy) against the Romance toponym reflexes (Játiva, Elche with initial stress) — the two authors read these opposite ways.

3842.tone: Flassy & Animung 1992 treat Iha as a stress language; the sections reached (§4.3, §5.4.1 and the §5.4 suprasegmental list: tekanan, glotalisasi, nasalisasi, uvularisasi) mention no tone or pitch accent. Second-hand: Cottet 2015 (Mbaham thesis, TEXT file) reports that Donohue (2005:48) assigns the whole West Bomberai group (Iha, Mbaham, Karas) a pitch-accent system and that Donohue & Gregory (2014, ANU talk) hypothesise contrastive grammatical tones carried by Iha suffixes and realised on the stem, with minimal functional load. 3847.prule: No word-stress position stated by any source. Ikposo is described as a tone language: Wolf 1909 §9 marks high tone (acute) and low tone (grave) and treats tone ('Tonakzente') as grammatical on the preterite infix (p. 631); Anderson 1999 gives H, M, L plus a lower-mid after H and two falling tones; Soubrier 2007 gives four level tones H, M, M2, L plus falling for the Uwi dialect of Doumé, with lexical tone classes on nouns (HH, HM2, HL, MM, LL, MF...) and a rising tone on unprefixed verbs that may be demarcative; Dozeman & Koufedji 2015 give low/mid/high with tone as meaning-bearing. The only intensity-accent remark is Wolf 1909 §6: in a heterosyllabic vowel sequence (ia, ie, iu, oa, oe, ue) 'as a rule the second vowel carries the dynamic accent' -- a statement about hiatus sequences, not a placement rule for the word.

3847.tone: Tone language by every source. Wolf 1909 §9 (p. 147): 'Intonation kommt im Ikposo vor', high tone marked with acute and low tone with grave; p. 631 uses 'Tonakzente... Tief- und Hochton' for the tones the preterite infix takes over from the 2nd/3rd person pronouns, so his §6 'dynamischer Akzent' (intensity) is a notion he keeps distinct from tone. Anderson 1999 sect. 2.3: three contrastive level tones H, M, L plus a lower-mid after H and two falling tones; the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur in the article. Soubrier 2007 chap. IV (Uwi, Doumé): four level tones H, M, M2, L and a falling tone; a rising tone occurs almost only on verbs without person/TAM prefixes and 'pourrait être avant tout démarcatif'; English initial stress in loans is rendered as the HL tone scheme (p. 44), and 'accent' is used in the thesis only for English. Dozeman & Koufedji 2015 p. 5: tonal, low/mid/high and combinations, tone unmarked in the orthography. No source gives an Ikposo stress or accent placement rule beyond Wolf's hiatus remark.

3849.prule: Fixed initial accent: the free PIE word accent fixed on the first syllable of every word (Krahe, hedged 'vielleicht'; Katičić 'one has only to suppose an initial accentuation'), inferred from the Albanian and Italian reflexes of ancient toponyms (Dyrrachium > Durrës, Isamnus > Ishëm, Drivastum > Drisht, Messapic Brundisium > Brindisi) and from medial syncope in names. Neroznak 1978 describes the same toponymic evidence as proparoxytone (antepenultimate) accent; the two framings coincide for the trisyllabic examples and differ only for four-syllable Dyrrachium.
3849.srule: Not mentioned in Katičić 1976 (ch. 'Illyrian', p. 186), Krahe 1943 (§10 pp. 33-35) or Neroznak 1978 (p. 162): the sources state only a hypothesised (initial / proparoxytone) position of the word accent for this extinct, textless language and say nothing about non-primary stresses.

3849.idn: Katičić 1976 describes Illyrian proper (toponyms of the Albanian coast and western Balkans), i.e. this language. Krahe 1943, whose §10 sentence supplies the word-domain quote and the 'first syllable of every word' generalization, uses 'Illyrisch' in his pan-Illyrian sense that counts Messapic and Venetic as Illyrian…
3849.exq_: No exceptions are mentioned in Katičić, Krahe or Neroznak; Krahe hedges the whole attribution to Illyrian with 'vielleicht auch das Illyrische' and Katičić with 'One has only to suppose', which is a hedge on the hypothesis, not a statement of exceptions.
3849.tone: No tone or pitch-accent claim; Krahe treats the inherited PIE accent as free and Illyrian as one of the languages that fixed it initially.
3849.exc_quote: No exceptional word, word class, loan stratum or affix is mentioned anywhere (Krahe §10; Katičić p. 186; Neroznak p. 162). 3856.prule: The tonic accent stays invariably on the principal root of the word; a word built from several roots carries one tonic accent per root, so a word has one, two or more accents. Because the language is prefixing and the principal root is generally the last syllable of the word (p. 4), the accent of a single-root word normally falls on the final syllable (kètsuè 'perro', accent on the final e). Position is set by morpheme identity (root vs. prefix/particle), not by syllable count or weight.
3856.srule: No secondary stress described; additional accents only in multi-root words: a word formed from several roots carries the tonic accent on each root, 'de lo que resulta que una palabra tiene uno, dos y mas acentos' (tchintsi tiòhò 'enredar': tsi and hó; tchininkià nawi 'envenenar': kiá and wi), with no ranking among them. Single-root words have one accent (on the root).

3857.dq: Prosodic words in Iquito are defined as the domain for stress and tone assignment and as the unit which must satisfy the bimoraic minimum word requirement. [fn. 1, p. 66] ... The Iquito word prosodic system consists of clearly distinguishable stress and tone systems, in which stress and tone have distinct acoustic correlates. [p. 54]
3857.dloc: §4 'Iquito stress', pp. 57-59; prosodic-word definition fn. 1, p. 66; stress correlates pp. 59-61; previous analyses §6, pp. 70-72.
3857.heavy: C(y)V: syllables (long vowel, with or without a palatal glide) are heavy; the language has no closed syllables, so vowel length is the only weight contrast.
3857.dflt: Penultimate syllable (head of the rightmost bimoraic trochee): (ˈa.ʃi), (ˌsa)(ˈtaki), (ˌku.ma)(ˈki.ha), nu(ˌtaki)(ˈnaka), (ˌkana)(ˌnahu)(ˈkura).
3857.prule: Feet are bimoraic (moraic) trochees parsed exhaustively right-to-left over the prosodic word; a long-vowel syllable C(y)V: is heavy, is always stressed and forms its own foot; the head of the rightmost foot carries primary stress. So primary stress is penultimate when the last two syllables are light ((ˈa.ʃi), (ˌku.ma)(ˈki.ha)), final when the final syllable is heavy (nu(ˌta.ku)(ˈrɨɨ), (ˌii)(ˈpɨɨ)), and on a heavy penult before a light final, which forms a trimoraic (ˈHL) foot rather than a final degenerate foot ((ˈsaa.pi)). Degenerate (monomoraic) feet are never built at the right edge (*(ˌL)(ˈL), *(ˌH)(ˈL)). Stress is diagnosed by tapping tasks and by lengthening of the post-tonic consonant, not by pitch.

3857.tone: Iquito also has a low-density privative H/ø tone system on the mora (§5, pp. 62-69), with lexical tonal minimal pairs. Every prosodic word must carry at least one H; when the rightmost colon has no lexical H, a metrical H is assigned to the primary-stressed syllable. The author separates the two systems by their correlates (pitch vs. post-tonic consonant lengthening) and notes that pitch peaks and primary stress need not coincide (p. 59). The 2019/2022 ILDP dictionaries revise the tonal analysis (H/L/null, HLL melodies) but say nothing about stress placement.

tn.quote: Iquito exhibits a H/ø privative tone system in which the tone bearing unit is the mora. Moras are thus either specified as bearing a high tone, or are unspecified for tone. Most moras are in fact unspecified for tone ... All prosodic words in Iquito exhibit at least a single high tone, and if a given prosodic word lacks lexically specified high tones (a common occurrence), a high tone is assigned to the syllable bearing primary stress. In this way, the tonal system is partially dependent on the stress system of the language for meeting an obligatory tone requirement.
tn.cite: Michael, Lev (2011). The interaction of tone and stress in the prosodic system of Iquito (Zaparoan). Amerindia 35: 53-74.
